summary: This informational document records how the IP service model has changed and what upper layers and applications can expect from it. It highlights properties that were wrongly assumed and properties that would cause trouble if changed. It is a reflective overview rather than a protocol.

eli5.summary: People have long guessed what the internet's delivery service promises, and some guesses were wrong. This writes down what it really does and how that changed.

questions: what does the ip service model guarantee
evolution of the internet protocol model
subtitle: What the IP service model actually promises—and how those promises have changed.

tldr.problem: Applications often make assumptions about IP's reliability, symmetry, and stability that were true in the early Internet but are no longer valid. These broken assumptions cause subtle bugs and security failures.
tldr.mechanism: The document catalogs eleven common misconceptions about IP—what packets promise, what addresses mean, whether multicast works, whether packets can be modified—and explains why each assumption fails in today's networks.
tldr.outcome: Protocol designers and developers can use this to build correct applications and protocols that do not depend on assumptions that NATs, firewalls, and routing policies have already broken.

today: RFC 6250 is an Informational document from the Internet Architecture Board that documents assumptions that were wrongly held about IP. It has not been obsoleted and remains a critical reference for protocol designers who need to understand which properties of IP can actually be relied upon in today's Internet.

sections.title: How the IP Service Model Has Changed
sections.content:
Since the Internet Protocol was first published in 1978, it has provided a network-layer connectivity service to upper-layer protocols and applications. The basic IP service model was documented in the original specifications, but over 30 years the actual service evolved significantly to enable new behaviors the original definition did not envision. By 1989, RFC 1122 already had to clarify many things and extend the model. Today's IP service model is not well documented in a single place; it is spread across many different RFCs.

As a result, today's IP service model is often misunderstood. This is dangerous: many applications and protocols rely on assumptions about IP that are no longer true. Network Address Translators (NATs), firewalls, routing policies, and wireless technologies have all changed what IP actually delivers. Understanding the evolution is critical to avoid building broken protocols and applications.
sections.eli5: The internet has changed a lot. What it promises today is different from what it promised 30 years ago. We should all know what changed.

sections.title: Broken Routing Assumptions
sections.content:
Many applications assume reachability is symmetric: if host A can contact host B, then B can respond to A. This was originally true, but NATs and firewalls break it. Today a request can get through, but an unsolicited request in the other direction may not. Applications also assume reachability is transitive: if A reaches B and B reaches C, then A reaches C. This remains true within a link but fails across the Internet when routing policies and firewalls divide the network.

Applications incorrectly assume ICMP error messages will arrive in response to bad packets. Many firewalls block ICMP and many routers rate-limit responses to prevent denial-of-service attacks. Some applications assume multicast works within a link, but Non-Broadcast Multi-Access (NBMA) links like X.25, ATM, and frame relay do not support it. Others assume IPv4 broadcast is available, but it has been deprecated for security reasons.

Applications pick the first host to respond to a request and assume that host is typical. This fails when the first packet takes an unusual path or path switching occurs after the first packet. Reordering is assumed rare, but per-packet load balancing and protocol path-switching cause it frequently. Loss is assumed probabilistic, not deterministic, but resolution queues at the last hop can cause deterministic packet drops for burst traffic.
sections.eli5: Applications assume messages always get there from both directions, that responses come back, that error messages arrive, and that packet order stays the same. None of these are always true anymore.

sections.title: Broken Addressing Assumptions
sections.content:
Many applications assume addresses are stable, but DHCP, roaming, and wireless have made addresses temporary. Applications cache DNS results without knowing their lifetime, causing problems when addresses become stale. An address is four bytes long is assumed by old code, but IPv6 addresses are 16 bytes, breaking four-byte-only implementations. A host has only one address on one interface was never true, but it was common; today hosts routinely have multiple IPv6 addresses on one interface.

Applications assume a non-multicast address identifies a single host over time, but anycast allows one address to represent multiple hosts, and DHCP reassigns addresses. An address indicates physical location, but tunneling and large-scale NATs make location inference unreliable. The address an application sees is the same as the routing address, but Mobile IPv6, HIP, and many other protocols deliberately break this for flexibility.

Other assumptions also fail: a subnet is smaller than or equal to a link, binding to an address binds to a specific interface, and every address is part of an on-link subnet prefix have all become less reliable in modern networks. Applications that depend on these will fail in edge cases.
sections.eli5: Addresses used to be stable and unique and tied to one device. They are not anymore. Old applications that guess the rules break.

sections.title: Extensibility and Security Misconceptions
sections.content:
The original IP design allowed new transport-layer protocols to work across the Internet by supporting many protocol numbers. But NATs and firewalls today only allow TCP, UDP, or HTTP, breaking this assumption. Even within TCP and UDP, if one stream between a pair of addresses works, then another should, but per-stream state in middleboxes can cause selective blocking.

Regarding security, applications assume packets are unmodified in transit, but NATs and other middleboxes modify content. They assume packets are private, but old protocols transmitted passwords in the clear and many still do. They assume source addresses are not forged, making them vulnerable to reflection attacks. IPsec provides solutions to these problems but is not widely deployed.
sections.eli5: IP lets you add new protocols, but middleboxes block them. Packets can be changed in flight. Attackers can fake source addresses. Old applications that trust these do not work anymore.

sections.title: Guidance for Designers and Developers
sections.content:
The document emphasizes several principles. Applications should use names rather than addresses. Many APIs unnecessarily expose addresses when applications already use domain names. This tightly couples applications to specific IP addresses, making them fragile.

When building protocols and applications, designers should be liberal in what effects they accept but conservative in what effects they cause. That is, tolerate diversity in the network but do not assume behaviors that middleboxes might break. Applications should be IP-version agnostic: design them to work with IPv4, IPv6, and addresses in general, not hard-coded to one version. Document the contract between layers: lower-layer protocols should state what assumptions upper layers can rely on; upper layers should document what they depend on from below.

Changes to the service model should be carefully evaluated for impact on existing applications. Historically, changes have been made without regard to such considerations, making the situation for applications today already problematic. The key to maintaining an interoperable Internet is documenting and maintaining invariants that higher layers can depend on and being very judicious with changes.
sections.eli5: Use names instead of addresses in applications. Design for both IPv4 and IPv6. Document what your protocol promises. Change carefully, so you do not break the thousands of programs using the internet.
